claims.text: The target material is a conventionally sintered W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
The proposed intervention is post-sintering hot isostatic pressing at elevated temperature and pressure.
Post-sintering HIP will suppress phase separation in the W–Cu composite.
Post-sintering HIP will heal interfacial voids in the W–Cu composite.
HIP conditions can promote interfacial diffusion without causing excessive grain growth.
HIP enhances W–Cu interfacial bonding and densification.
Enhanced interfacial bonding and densification reduce the microvoid volume fraction.
Enhanced interfacial bonding and densification inhibit phase separation between W and Cu.
Elevated temperature and pressure during HIP promote atomic diffusion across W–Cu interfaces.
Atomic diffusion across W–Cu interfaces heals microvoids.
Improved interfacial connectivity creates a more continuous thermal-conduction pathway.
The HIP-induced microstructure mitigates the detrimental effects of irradiation-induced void formation during service.
After identical heat-transfer and irradiation exposure, the HIP-treated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
After identical heat-transfer and irradiation exposure, the HIP-treated composite will have a lower interfacial void fraction than the untreated composite.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to sintered W–Cu composites used under service environments similar to joints between W plasma-facing components and Cu cooling components.
HIP is known to reduce porosity in many composites.
Direct evidence connecting HIP-induced interfacial healing to improved W–Cu performance under simultaneous heat-transfer and irradiation conditions is limited.
